dossiers.title: Sex with Stalin
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 8 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The core interaction is a largely static dialogue-choice visual novel in which branching answers determine absurd alternate-history endings, rather than action-based gameplay.
One Russian player reports enjoying the polished voice work and eccentric premise after completing every branch; the unusual humor is a central attraction.
Players react to the intentionally provocative historical-comedy setup mainly as satire or a novelty, with enjoyment depending heavily on tolerance for exaggerated jokes.
A completed-playthrough account found multiple paths and endings amusing to collect, while another player described long, unskippable dialogue as tiring relative to the payoffs.
Repeated conversations and replaying choice paths are the main means of exploring outcomes; this supports ending hunting but makes repeat play text-heavy.
The title's shock-value expectations differ from its actual focus on comic dialogue, political caricature and brief divergent finales, frustrating some who expect a different genre.
A community ending guide maps many different choice sequences, illustrating that exploration is chiefly about branching story outcomes rather than numerical character development.
A buyer who tried the game reported that early dialogue was not conveniently skippable and that some endings felt less rewarding than the amount of reading required.

dossiers.title: Alan Wake
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 10 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Combat requires stripping shadow protection with a flashlight or other light source before firearms can damage enemies; this makes light an unusual tactical resource.
The mystery of a writer, missing family member and an uncanny town is delivered through TV-style episodes, manuscript pages, narration and cliffhangers, strongly attracting story-focused players.
Players praise the eerie forests and small-town atmosphere, ambient and licensed music and presentation inspired by mystery television and supernatural thrillers.
A frequently repeated complaint is that successive forest encounters reuse the same shine-light-then-shoot loop with little enemy variety, reducing the appeal of a long campaign.

Combat frustration is tied to the dodge and aiming feel, interruptions to reload or change equipment, abrupt weapon resets and large enemy waves; some players suggest easier difficulty to prioritize the story.
The campaign alternates daytime character interaction and nighttime action while advancing a serialized mystery, but players dispute whether the later chase sections overstay their welcome.
Discoverable manuscript pages and optional collectibles add foreshadowing and story context, with completion-focused players noting additional achievement challenges.
Using batteries, safe light zones, flares and occasional powerful light weapons changes resource management, while some players feel repeated encounters test patience more than mastery.
The original PC edition's additional special episodes offer extra story after the six-episode main campaign, yet a player considers one bonus episode less satisfying than the other.
An individual player disliked the infrequent vehicle sections and limited movement responsiveness, while valuing the flashlight as an atmospheric tool.

dossiers.title: Crysis 2 - Maximum Edition
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 10 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The Nanosuit shifts between armor and cloaking, letting players alternate stealth, mobility and direct gunfights; several describe satisfying flexible FPS encounters.
New York skyscrapers, subway spaces and collapsing urban set pieces replace the first game's wide jungle areas; the urban spectacle is praised despite a more scripted route structure.
Visual effects, cinematic urban destruction and a memorable soundtrack are repeatedly singled out as durable strengths of the original PC release.
Alien-derived suit upgrades let players specialize modules, yet some report relying heavily on camouflage and armor rather than experimenting with the full upgrade menu.
Some players say invisibility can trivialize encounters and enemy AI is inconsistent; others enjoy the combination of enemy waves and tactical positioning.
Complaints include occasional unclear objectives and corridors, long checkpoint setbacks, and weaker physics or environmental destructibility than the first Crysis.
The campaign alternates human PMC fights and alien battles in a story-led urban thriller; players disagree on whether its higher cinematic pacing offsets reduced freedom.

This Maximum Edition includes extra multiplayer maps and weapons, but player reports from 2017 onward say its old multiplayer ecosystem was already inactive or inaccessible; this is a historical access warning, not a verified live-server claim.
Player reaction to the story and protagonist is mixed: some find the New York invasion absorbing, while others miss characters and open-ended encounters from the earlier game.
Even when the shooting feels responsive, extended scripted firefights and overpowered suit strategies can reduce variety compared with the franchise's earlier sandbox style.
